analysis.one_liner: Lets states waive Affordable Care Act rules and turn insurance subsidies into health savings accounts.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Senator Rick Scott with two Republican cosponsors, has sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote since November 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let states waive core Affordable Care Act rules — including the list of benefits every plan must cover and the cost-sharing reductions that lower out-of-pocket costs for lower-income enrollees — provided the state maintains a high-risk insurance pool. Federal subsidies would instead be paid as cash into "Trump Health Freedom Accounts" (a type of health savings account), with amounts capped at a national average premium rather than the state's actual prices. It would also let insurers sell plans across waiver states, expand a small-business insurance tax credit, bar using the account money for abortion services or a long list of procedures defined as gender transition care, and tighten hospital price transparency requirements.
analysis.who_benefits: Healthy, younger enrollees in states that take a waiver could buy cheaper plans that don't have to cover the ACA's full benefit list, and eligible residents who enroll through an exchange would see their federal subsidy dollars deposited as cash into a Trump Health Freedom Account they can use for premiums and medical bills. Small employers in waiver states would get a 50% insurance tax credit with no phaseout, no two-year expiration, no wage rule, and eligibility doubled to 50 employees. Insurers would gain freedom to design narrower plans, sell them across all waiver states, and offer child-only plans; banks and financial firms would administer the new accounts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Healthy enrollees, small employers, insurers, HSA providers

how_it_helps.text: Residents of waiver states who enroll through an exchange would receive the premium tax credit and cost-sharing reduction money they would otherwise get deposited directly into a health savings account, paid monthly, quarterly, or in a lump sum, and usable to buy health insurance or pay medical bills.

States could waive the ACA's market rules (Parts 1 and 2 of subtitle D), the cost-sharing reduction program, and the premium tax credit and individual mandate, while a separate subsection locks in pre-existing condition protections, guaranteed issue, guaranteed renewability, and the ban on annual and lifetime limits under title XXVII of the Public Health Service Act.

Small employers in waiver states would get a 50% health insurance tax credit with no phaseout, no cap on how long it lasts, no average-wage requirement, and eligibility expanded to 50 employees, applying to any state-authorized plan rather than only exchange plans.

Health plans authorized in any waiver state could be sold on the exchanges or private 'commercial platforms' of every other waiver state, and states could let private companies run their marketplaces using the federal exchange's technology.

Hospitals and insurers would have to disclose actual prices rather than estimates, in a standardized, comparable format, with updated enforcement, and providers would have to publicly report outcomes data.

analysis.who_pays: Sicker and older residents of waiver states would bear the gap between a fixed subsidy — calculated from a national average silver premium, not their state's actual prices — and what coverage really costs where they live, and plans would no longer have to cover the ACA's essential benefits, so comprehensive coverage could shrink or disappear from their market. Taxpayers would fund the account deposits and the expanded, unlimited small-employer credit. People who need abortion services or any procedure on the bill's long defined list of gender transition care — which includes vasectomy, tubal ligation, and sterilization — could not use their own federal subsidy dollars to pay for them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sicker, older enrollees in waiver states

drawbacks.text: Subsidy amounts would be based on the national average premium for a silver plan among non-waiver states, so residents of high-premium states could receive substantially less help than they do today, and the money would have to cover both premiums and out-of-pocket costs from a single account.

States could waive the essential health benefit rules, meaning plans would no longer have to cover required categories such as prescription drugs, maternity care, or mental health treatment — people needing comprehensive coverage could be left with thinner options or none.

The ban on using account funds for the defined 'gender transition procedures' sweeps in vasectomy, tubal ligation, and sterilization generally, so common reproductive health care could not be paid for with these federal dollars, alongside a blanket ban on abortion services.

A waiver lasts indefinitely — it continues until the state that requested it opts out — and the condition attached to it, an 'invisible high-risk insurance pool,' is undefined, with no standard for how much risk the state must absorb or how it keeps premiums affordable for sick enrollees.

The bill text contains no estimates of what the account deposits and the unlimited small-employer credit would cost the Treasury, and no analysis of how many people would end up with less coverage than they have under current law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The price transparency provisions — actual prices, standardized and comparable, with outcomes reporting — are a real gain for consumers that both parties have supported in some form. The core redesign is riskier: it converts income-based subsidies that adjust to local premiums into fixed cash accounts and lets states drop the benefit requirements that make insurance comprehensive. That combination tends to favor people who are young, healthy, and higher-income, while sicker, older, and lower-income enrollees — especially in high-premium states — would likely get less workable coverage. The account-use bans and the unlimited small-employer credit are major policy choices attached with no cost or coverage analysis anywhere in the record, so the trade-offs cannot be assessed from the bill itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Finance Committee, where it has had no hearing, vote, or other action so far.

narrative.text: Senator Rick Scott of Florida introduced the bill on November 20, 2025, with two Republican cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which handles tax and health legislation.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and Congress remains in session until January 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet: the bill has only been referred to committee, so current Affordable Care Act rules and subsidies still apply unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; current rules still apply

for.name: Sen. Rick Scott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which bears his health freedom waiver and 'Trump Health Freedom Accounts' design.

for.name: Two Republican senators
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No one has voted on the bill; all three senators attached to it are Republicans, and no opponent has acted on it in the record.

industries.note: In waiver states, insurers could sell plans that skip the ACA's required benefits, offer child-only plans, and sell state-authorized plans across all waiver states. Some consumers would get cheaper options, but the plans would cover less, and the burden of sick enrollees would shift to whatever 'invisible high-risk pool' a state sets up.

industries.industry: Banks and health savings account administrators
industries.note: The bill creates a new class of federally funded accounts and requires subsidy deposits into them, generating a new book of accounts to administer. Enrollees keep the money, but a new financial intermediary stands between them and their coverage.

In waiver states, small employers could claim a 50% insurance tax credit with no phaseout, no two-year limit, no wage rule, and eligibility expanded from 25 to 50 employees — a much richer benefit than current law.

Providers would face new requirements to publish actual prices in a standardized format, face updated enforcement for compliance, and publicly report outcomes data. Patients gain visibility into prices; providers lose pricing opacity and take on compliance costs.

industries.industry: Providers of gender-affirming and reproductive care
industries.note: Account funds could not pay for abortion services or for the bill's long defined list of 'gender transition procedures,' which includes vasectomy, tubal ligation, and sterilization. Patients using these accounts could not spend their own federal subsidy dollars on those services.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is two days old in a committee that takes up only a small share of referred bills. With a single sponsor, two cosponsors, and no hearing or committee action on the record, its likely path is to sit in the Senate Finance Committee unless the chairman or Senate leadership chooses to move it; most bills at this stage never reach a floor vote before the Congress ends.
